questions.question_text: An economy produces only guns and butter. If it is operating ON its production possibilities curve, producing more guns requires:
questions.option_b: Giving up some butter — an opportunity cost
questions.option_c: No trade-off, since resources are unlimited
questions.option_d: A rightward shift of the curve
questions.explanation: On the PPC, all resources are employed — more of one good means less of the other. A point INSIDE the curve allows more of both (unemployed resources); shifting the curve requires growth in resources or technology, not a production choice.

questions.question_text: Which transaction is included in this year's U.S. GDP?
questions.option_a: Buying a used 2019 car from a dealer
questions.option_b: A new car produced and sold this year
questions.option_d: A Social Security payment to a retiree
questions.explanation: GDP counts NEW final goods and services produced this year. Used goods were counted when new; stocks are asset swaps, not production; transfer payments produce nothing. (The used-car dealer's markup — the service — does count, but not the car itself.)

questions.question_text: Nominal GDP rose 6% while the GDP deflator rose 4%. Real GDP grew approximately:
questions.explanation: Real growth ≈ nominal growth − inflation = 6% − 4% = 2%. Nominal GDP conflates production with prices; the deflator strips out the price change. Adding instead of subtracting (option A) reverses the logic.

questions.question_text: A discouraged worker who stopped searching for jobs last month causes the official unemployment rate to:
questions.option_b: Fall, because he leaves the labor force and is no longer counted as unemployed
questions.explanation: Unemployment = (jobless AND actively searching) ÷ labor force. Quitting the search removes him from both the numerator and the labor force — mechanically LOWERING the rate even though the economy didn't improve. This is why falling unemployment can mask labor-market weakness.

questions.question_text: A software engineer laid off because her skills were replaced by AI tools experiences which type of unemployment?
questions.explanation: A mismatch between workers' skills and what the economy demands = structural. Frictional is ordinary between-jobs searching; cyclical follows the business cycle. Structural unemployment persists even in expansions — that's the distinguishing test.

questions.question_text: Unexpected inflation generally benefits:
questions.explanation: Borrowers repay in dollars worth LESS than expected — the real burden of fixed-rate debt shrinks. Lenders, cash-holders, and fixed-wage workers all lose purchasing power. Key word: UNEXPECTED; anticipated inflation gets priced into interest rates.

questions.question_text: A sharp rise in oil prices shifts short-run aggregate supply left. The result is:
questions.option_a: Higher price level and higher real GDP
questions.option_b: Lower price level and lower real GDP
questions.option_c: Higher price level and lower real GDP — stagflation
questions.option_d: Lower price level and higher real GDP
questions.explanation: Supply shocks move price level and output in OPPOSITE directions — the stagflation case (1970s). This is also the policy dilemma: fighting inflation deepens the recession; fighting unemployment fuels inflation. Demand shifts move them in the same direction.

questions.question_text: With MPC = 0.8, a $100 billion increase in government spending raises real GDP by at most:
questions.explanation: Spending multiplier = 1/(1−MPC) = 1/0.2 = 5 → $500B. Note the TAX-cut multiplier is smaller (MPC/(1−MPC) = 4 → $400B, option D) because the first round of a tax cut is partly saved. Knowing which multiplier applies is the real question.

questions.question_text: Crowding out occurs when expansionary fiscal policy financed by borrowing:
questions.option_a: Raises interest rates, reducing private investment
questions.explanation: Government borrowing increases demand for loanable funds → real interest rates rise → some private investment is priced out. Part of the fiscal stimulus is offset. Graph it in the loanable funds market: demand shifts right, equilibrium r rises.

questions.question_text: With a required reserve ratio of 10%, a new $1,000 deposit can expand the money supply by a MAXIMUM of:
questions.option_b: $9,000 in new loans, $10,000 total including the deposit
questions.option_d: $10,000 in new loans on top of the deposit
questions.explanation: Money multiplier = 1/0.10 = 10 → total money $10,000, of which $9,000 is NEWLY CREATED through lending ($1,000 already existed as the deposit). The exam asks both versions — read whether it wants 'new money created' or 'total.'

questions.question_text: To fight a recession, the Federal Reserve would most likely:
questions.option_b: Buy government bonds, increasing bank reserves and lowering interest rates
questions.explanation: Open-market PURCHASES inject reserves → more lending → lower interest rates → more investment and consumption. The other three all CONTRACT the money supply. Mnemonic: the Fed BUYS bonds to BOOST the economy.

questions.question_text: In the long run, an increase in the money supply primarily causes:
questions.option_c: A proportionally higher price level with real output back at potential
questions.option_d: A permanent fall in nominal interest rates
questions.explanation: Money neutrality: long-run output is pinned by resources and technology, so money growth ends up in prices (and via the Fisher effect, HIGHER nominal rates, not lower). The short-run boost evaporates as wages and expectations adjust — that's the whole point of the LRAS being vertical.

questions.question_text: The short-run Phillips curve shows a trade-off between inflation and unemployment, but the long-run Phillips curve is vertical because:
questions.option_a: Inflation and unemployment always move together
questions.option_b: In the long run, expectations adjust and unemployment returns to its natural rate at any inflation level
questions.option_c: Monetary policy is ineffective in the short run
questions.option_d: The natural rate of unemployment is zero
questions.explanation: Workers and firms build expected inflation into wages, undoing the short-run trade-off — leaving unemployment at the natural rate regardless of the inflation rate. A supply shock shifts the SRPC; expectations shifts move it back. The LRPC sits at the natural rate, never zero.

questions.question_text: An increase in household saving shifts the loanable funds supply curve right. The equilibrium result is:
questions.option_a: Higher real interest rate, less investment
questions.option_b: Lower real interest rate, more investment
questions.option_d: No change in the interest rate
questions.explanation: More saving = more funds supplied → the price of borrowing (real interest rate) falls → firms invest more. This is the market mechanism connecting thrift today to capital formation and growth tomorrow.

questions.question_text: If U.S. interest rates rise relative to Europe's, the U.S. dollar will most likely:
questions.option_b: Appreciate, as foreign investors demand dollars to buy U.S. assets
questions.option_d: Be devalued by the Federal Reserve
questions.explanation: Higher returns attract foreign financial capital → investors must BUY dollars → dollar appreciates. Chain: interest rates → capital flows → currency demand. A stronger dollar then makes U.S. exports pricier — the follow-up the FRQ usually asks.

questions.question_text: A country runs a current account deficit. Its capital and financial account must be:
questions.option_b: In surplus of roughly the same magnitude
questions.explanation: The balance of payments balances: importing more than you export means foreigners end up holding your currency/assets — recorded as financial account inflows. CA deficit ≡ KA surplus. They're two sides of one ledger, not independent quantities.

questions.question_text: Which policy most directly increases an economy's long-run aggregate supply?
questions.option_a: A one-time tax rebate to consumers
questions.option_c: An increase in the money supply
questions.explanation: LRAS shifts with productive capacity: human capital, physical capital, technology. Rebates and money growth move DEMAND (short-run); tariffs reallocate rather than expand capacity. Growth policy = supply-side capacity building.

questions.question_text: The economy is in a recessionary gap. With NO policy action, the classical self-correction mechanism predicts:
questions.option_a: Wages eventually fall, shifting SRAS right until output returns to potential
questions.option_d: LRAS shifts left to meet current output
questions.explanation: High unemployment puts downward pressure on nominal wages → lower production costs → SRAS shifts right → price level falls, output recovers. Keynes's objection was the SPEED ('in the long run we are all dead') — not the mechanism's existence.

questions.question_text: Which function of money does inflation most directly erode?
questions.explanation: Inflation shrinks what saved money will buy later — attacking its ability to STORE value over time. Money may still circulate fine as a medium of exchange in moderate inflation; hyperinflation eventually destroys all three functions.

questions.question_text: Which is an automatic stabilizer?
questions.option_a: Congress passing an emergency stimulus bill
questions.option_b: Unemployment insurance payouts rising as layoffs increase during a recession
questions.explanation: Automatic stabilizers kick in WITHOUT new legislation — UI payouts and progressive taxes expand deficits in downturns by design. Options A and D are discretionary fiscal policy (require action); C is monetary policy. 'No vote needed' is the test.
